utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. May we have the appearances now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Teresa McHenry for the Prosecution, along with Mr. Turone and Mr. Huber. Mr. Niemann is another courtroom and will join us later in the day. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: May we have appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I am Edina Residovic, Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic, along with my colleague, Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning Your Honours, Tomslav Kuzmanovic along with our legal assistant, Niko Djuric, on behalf of defendant, Zdravko Mucic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour, I am Salih Karabdic, Defence counsel for Mr. Hazim Delic, along with Mr. Tom Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, my name is Nancy Boler, I represent Esad Landzo, along with Cynthia McMurrey, who will be joining us in a few hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms. McHenry, you're still cross-examining. May we have the witness now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, before we bring the witness, there's a couple of short housekeeping matters I would like to bring to the trial chamber's attention. The first is the request for subpoena on Mr. Ustalic and his wife won't let him come without a subpoena. Will the Trial Chamber please entertain issuing that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We'll try and ensure that it's issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And the other housekeeping matter is this: We have a tape of one of the prosecutor's witnesses being interviewed on television. And there is some question over the date that this occurred. Our information is that the tape was on February 17th,'97, approximately a month before the witness testified. The Prosecutor is unsure. That is the subpoena we requested for Belgrade Television. We would re-urge that subpoena and I would also inform the Court that my secretary in the States is trying to see if there is some way that there is a company in America that downloads these things from satellite and then rebroadcasts them through cable television. We're trying to authenticate it that way, but I think we need to re-urge the subpoena for Belgrade Television just to prove the date. The Prosecution tells me that in good faith they cannot stipulate to the date and it is a fairly important piece of evidence for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: In that respect, you do your homework and then make the proper application.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Well, we've already requested that subpoena and I just wanted to re-urge it and to inform the Court what we're doing so that, you know, you understand that we're trying everything in good faith and why we're seeking these two subpoenas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I just say one thing. I would just like to concur with Mr. Moran's opinion that a subpoena will be necessary for Mr. Ustalic. I spoke to him in Konjic when I was there yesterday and he tells me that his mother is very frightened for him to leave, but he's on our witness list as well. So I concur with Mr. Moran's opinion about a subpoena for Mr. Ustalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly swear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: May I remind the witness that he's still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Ms. McHenry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, are you sure that you were at the camp until the end of June or could it have been earlier that you left?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Until the end of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, you stated yesterday that there were no other members of Mr. Landzo's family who worked in the camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, did you ever hear Mr. Landzo talk?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: With whom?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, let me just ask you, you would agree that Mr. Landzo has an unusual voice, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Would you -- have you ever heard Mr. Landzo say anything to anyone?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me just clarify an issue. Yesterday you stated in direct testimony, line 2746, that the commander of the HVO military police, when you were assigned to Celebici prison, was Mr. Alibasic. Now I now understand that when you said that, it was a mistake and you now say that Mr. Alibasic did not come to the camp until the time you left. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: After we left, he came.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did the War Presidency or the courts or the Ministry of Justice, did they have anything to do with the Celebici prison?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, given that there are a number of different entities in the camp, including the MUP, the TO and persons from the HVO, who was in charge of coordinating the activities of these different bodies as it related to the prison?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know what coordinator is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't ask you what a coordinator is, I asked you, given that there were a number of different entities there, I assume someone tried to coordinate their activities; is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: No, that's asking him who is the coordinator is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, sir, did any person or persons do anything to coordinate the activities of the different bodies who worked in Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Only whoever belonged to whatever group.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And was there anyone who was supposed to make sure that the groups worked together in running the camp? If you know.

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, you stated that you brought Mr. Cedo Antic and Mrs. Milojka Antic to their interrogations, so am I correct that in addition to your duties as a driver, you sometimes brought prisoners to be interrogated?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, you and Mr. Mucic do not have any dispute or bad relations between you, do you?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know why we would.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And as far as you know, you do not; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You're not aware of any bad relations between yourself and Mr. Mucic, are you?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I only saw Mucic once.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, now if Mr. Mucic gave a statement where he spoke about seeing you and Mr. Delic mistreat prisoners being brought for interrogations by beating them with a rifle butt and other things, would that have been the time that you saw Mr. Mucic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It was a little complex question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Ask him the first part of Mucic said this and then whether it was on that occasion because he doesn't know what to answer and what not to answer. So he will have a tendency to answer the latter part of your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Fair enough, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me, he answered the question, but it was not translated or recorded on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: All right. Let me just ask it again.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, were you and Mr. Delic beating prisoners who were brought for interrogation at the time that you saw Mr. Mucic?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, you would agree that it's possible that Mr. Mucic could see you on occasion in the camp when you didn't see him?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the question, it's asking him to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, are you able to answer that question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I renew my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It's a possibility that he could see him without him knowing it. There's nothing irregular about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, I assume you don't know why Mr. Mucic would say he saw you mistreating prisoners if it didn't happen?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I am going to object, it's asking him to figure out what Mr. Mucic said and asking him to inquire into Mr. Mucic's state of mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: He can answer to the best of his ability, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He said he doesn't know him. He's seen him only once. How can he figure why he should?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I assume he can say then he doesn't know why Mr. Mucic would have said this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Is it the case that you don't know why Mr. Mucic would say he saw you mistreating prisoners if it weren't true?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: But Miro Golubovic was imprisoned Tunnel No. 9, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Which Golubovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Miro Golubovic. Do you know a Miro Golubovic?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Barely.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And he was imprisoned in Tunnel No. 9, wasn't he, for at least part of the time that he was in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You once brought Mr. Golubovic a blanket and some toiletries, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And so I assume you also don't remember whether or not it was Mr. Mucic who told you to bring those items. I assume you don't remember. In fact, let me withdraw that question. Now, sir, the investigative commission stopped working while you were still in Celebici, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, did there come a time when they stopped coming to the camp, or you just don't remember?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't remember and I wasn't around all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, how much time did Mr. Musinovic spend in the camp?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know that person.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's probably my pronunciation, sir. Mr. Rale Musinovic, how much time did he spend in the camp?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: As much as I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Would he be there for most of the day?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: As needed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, would he usually just be there for a few minutes a day or for a large part of the day?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: As needed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, can you give us some idea of what was needed? I know it could change, but can you give us some idea, was he sometimes there most of the day, was he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is this witness in charge of this other gentleman?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No, he's not in charge of it, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Then how can he then tell you as many times as he would be needed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: He could certainly, I believe, tell me when he saw him there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What thing?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, do you have any idea, any information, about how much time Mr. Rale Musinovic spent in the camp?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think he's already answered that, he said as much as he had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He's being a little evasive, maybe sometimes he was there for the whole day, sometimes only for an hour. She wants to find out what was usually the time he spent in the camp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no need for me to write that or remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Is it then the case that you have no memory of how much time Mr. Musinovic spent in the camp?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: He had his duties and I had mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, I'll just take that as a "yes" then, sir. Did Mr. Musinovic have an office in the camp, and if so, where was his office?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: There were no offices there, just rooms for -- with beds where people slept.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, Mr. Musinovic did not have an office in the camp? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: It wasn't a real office.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was there a room where he spent most of his time when he was in the camp?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Very little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What are the duties of this Rale Musinovic? What are his duties? What does he do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He spent very little time there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: As what? Is he a fellow driver or is he somebody on some other duties in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the most part he dealt with logistics, provision of food and such. And he received orders from the superior command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And who was the superior command as you understood it?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Probably the MUP or the TO or the HVO, to whomever he belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Is it your testimony, sir, that you don't know to whom -- what entity Mr. Musinovic belonged?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I was not interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, when Mr. Musinovic was not in the camp, was there anyone else who took over his duties?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was there any other driver in the prison besides you?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. And who was that?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Zlatan Ustalic, Buric. There were several.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And Mr. Zlatan was in charge of driving the food; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And was there any difference between your duties and Mr. Buric's duties as drivers?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours. It should be Buric. I'm sorry, counsel, it's listed as "Boric". It should be "Buric" in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Once again, it's probably my pronunciation, so I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If I understood you, you were a driver and Mr. Buric was a driver. My question is: Was there any difference in your duties? How was it decided when you would drive and when he would drive and when one of you would do something else?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Apologies, Your Honours, the identical error occurred. Again we have "Boric" instead of Buric, B-U-R-I-C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I was driving our car of the MUP police.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And what car did Mr. Buric drive?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: You should ask him that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Does that mean you don't know, sir? If you don't know an answer to a question, sir, all you have to do is say "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did Mr. Buric work in the prison the whole time that you were working there?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. To your knowledge, was there any dispute between you or bad relations between you, between you and Mr. Buric?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, I know you stated that Mr. Delic was not a deputy commander, and I know that you stated that he was wounded and spent more or had an injury, and he spent more time sitting than standing. Do you know if Mr. Delic had any duties in the camp at all?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: At that time he didn't, except that he would sometimes keep guard and he would go with the doctors to the hospital, to the doctors who came to the camp, and he would sometimes bring milk to the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So sometimes --

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: And medicine.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So sometimes he acted as a guard, sometimes he went to the hospital, and sometimes he brought milk to the prisoners; is that correct? That's what you know about Mr. Delic's duties?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, is it your testimony, sir, that during the entire time you were at Celebici camp --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours. There is a mistake, a very important mistake, actually, as far as my client is concerned. The transcript says this is about Delic and it says "Delalic" in the transcript. I would like to ask you that these are corrected because it is very difficult for us to listen to the proceedings and watch the transcript at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, during the time that you were at Celebici, is it your testimony that you never saw any prisoner being mistreated?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you ever hear any screams or sounds of blows?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Never while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you ever see any prisoners with injuries on them?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Rarely, but only with those who came from the woods before, and before they came to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And how would you know when you saw a prisoner with injuries? How would you know that that's a prisoner who came from the woods?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: If they -- if I was there the day they appear -- came to the camp, it was easy to recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you ever hear any reports or rumours that any prisoners were being mistreated in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you mentioned building number 22. What was building -- was building 22 used as an infirmary when you were at the camp?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: It was an empty building.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, when you were at Celebici camp, there were no prisoners kept in building 22; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: When we came, there was nobody there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: When you left.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And when you left, was it the case that prisoners were not in 22 also?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't quite understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It's a very simple question. You said when you went to Celebici -- it's a very simple question. You were asked, did you find any people in this room number 22. You said when you went to the camp, there was none. She wants to find out when you left the camp to go somewhere else, were there any people there in this room number 22?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were. Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And was it injured people who were kept in building 22 or you don't know?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: They were not injured. They were sick. What they were sick from, I don't know. Natural diseases. It was an infirmary for them. There were doctors there. Two of their doctors were there and other doctors from Konjic would come if there was any need.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, besides Mr. Susic and the man who was shot trying to escape, did any other prisoners die during the time you worked in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, you talked some yesterday in direct about the conditions in Celebici, and I assume, since you testified about it, that you had the opportunity to observe the conditions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, you said the prison was not crowded. I mean the barracks were not crowded. Do you know why prisoners were kept in tunnel number 9?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: So that they would not get into touch with other prisoners before they were interrogated.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were prisoners kept in tunnel number 9 the entire time you worked in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And how was it you learned that this is the reason the prisoners were kept in tunnel number 9? Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: The reason was because they were brought there during the day and at night-time, and they were put there so that they couldn't hide anything before they were interrogated, before the commission would have the results.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: My question, sir, is how do you know that? Did someone tell you that or did you just make that assumption yourself? And if someone told you, who was it who told you?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Nobody told me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, please describe the conditions in the tunnel, what the conditions were like for the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: It was just like any other tunnel. Every prisoner had his own blanket and they were allowed to leave the tunnel. They had food, they had water, they had an outside toilet just behind the facility.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So, as far as you are concerned, the conditions in tunnel number 9 were fine?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Considering the circumstances, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, prisoners were sometimes placed in manholes, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, how often would the prisoners in both tunnel number 9 and in the hangar, how often would they be let outside to use the bathroom facilities, and how long would they have when they were allowed to go outside?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Whenever they wanted, there was a guard at the door. It was important to knock, and then they would go out.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So it's your testimony that whenever a prisoner wanted, all they had to do was knock on the door and then they could go use the facilities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And did they ever go out in groups also? Were there regular times that they went out in groups?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: If there was a need, yes. If there wasn't, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, did you ever see prisoners running to use the facilities?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, what if somebody was sick or injured and couldn't go -- couldn't go out themselves to use the bathroom, what were their facilities then?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: They would be taken outside, carried outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. And did you see that happen?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, how do you know that that's what happened, if you never saw it, sir? Did someone tell you that's what happened?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you also talked about the water. How did the prisoners get water?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Whenever they wanted, they could.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So they would just knock on the door and any of the 200 or 300 -- let me go back. How many prisoners were there in Celebici, approximately, as best you can estimate?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Would you agree that it was around 300?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the response. Could the witness please repeat.

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I never counted them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, however many there were, whenever the prisoners wanted water, all they had to do is knock on the door, say, "I want water," then they would be allowed outside to get water? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Inside the hangar, were the prisoners allowed to get up and move around however they liked, or did they have to stay seated?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Whatever they wanted to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And were the doors to the hangar usually kept open or closed?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Closed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. And did you also, when you say the prisoners were allowed to do whatever they wanted, is that something you saw yourself or something you heard?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I came to visit and I would bring them food from their families, and whenever I came some of them would be standing, some of them would be sitting, just like anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And how many times would you estimate that you yourself went into the hangar?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you ever go inside tunnel number 9?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Only to the entrance door.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, let's talk about the food. First of all, I assume that you sometimes ate meals outside the prison, like at your girlfriend's; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, who was Sok?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: A small -- a young Albanian who was in -- was in the JNA and then he stayed in the village. He joined us and he would sometimes make us coffee or prepare our meals or lunches.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: He worked as a cook in the camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, as an auxiliary cook.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And did he cook just for the guards or did he also cook for the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: The food was brought from the village -- from the city, and he would just distribute it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: When you said "he prepared our meals," you meant that he distributed your meals? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. He would distribute it to our dishes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And it's your testimony that he never actually cooked; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Rarely. Very rarely.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And on those rare occasions when he cooked something, was that just for the guards or was that for the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I ate his food rarely.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: How often was the food brought to the camp for the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Just like would happen for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. My question was how often? Was it every day?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Every day. Every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And was it once a day or more than once a day?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Sometimes it was once a day, both for us and for them, but most of the times it was more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And most of the time. Then how many times was it? Twice or more than twice?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Twice.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, when the food was brought, did it come in big containers or individual portions?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Big containers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And please just explain to us how the prisoners would get their food, where they would eat it, who would bring it to them. Did they eat at the same time? Can you just give us an idea about that?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: From every facility two or three inmates would come, they would pour the food into smaller containers, the same way it happened to us, and then they would distribute the food in front of the facilities where they were. They would hand out the plates to the inmates, and then they would later collect it and go back to their facility.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And would the prisoners eat all at once or would they eat in shifts?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: In shifts, because there weren't -- there wasn't enough -- there weren't enough plates.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. And, approximately, just how many plates were there? I mean, are we talking about five or one hundred?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Every facility had at least ten plates, and then these ten were distributed each time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. So if I understand you, ten prisoners would eat at one time? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, in front of one facility.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And let's at least talk about the hangar. And is it the case, then, that after ten prisoners would eat, somebody would go all the way back to the reception, the administration building and get more food, or how did that work?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: No. Everybody ate at the same time. Every facility had about ten plates and that's how they ate. Everybody simultaneously.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, how did -- if you just accept for a minute that there were, let's say, two hundred people in the hangars, how would those two hundred people eat from ten plates?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: There weren't -- there never were two hundred people in one hangar, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: But it's your testimony that however many people there were in the hangar, all of them would eat at the same time from the same ten containers?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Every facility had at least ten mess tins, at least, and then they would take turns. They would be washed and then food for the next ten prisoners would be dished out.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And would this happen immediately in front of the hangar, or would the prisoners have to go back to the administration building to get the additional food to fill up the containers again?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Sometimes they would go again and, if there was any food left, they would get it. Nothing was spilt.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And would they walk back to the administration building to get the extra food, or how did that work?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Sometimes they would use the car, sometimes they would walk.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. And about how long would this whole procedure take? The food would come in, be distributed, switch on and off. About how long would this take for all the prisoners to be fed?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Would you say it was more than an hour?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, would Mr. Ustalic stay until all the prisoners had finished eating?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Sometimes he would, sometimes he wouldn't. It was important to take the food.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, you stated yesterday that the prisoners got the same portions as the guards. How do you know that those prisoners got the same portions?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: It is true because I ate the same food.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: My question wasn't whether or not you ate the same food. My question was how much food, the portions. How do you know that the prisoners got the same portions as the guards?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I know sometimes I was there and I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. How often would you say you were present and would watch the prisoners eating and could see their portions, approximately?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: On several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, you talked yesterday about a prisoner who was shot when he was trying to escape. Now, were you present when that prisoner was shot or did someone else tell you about it?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I was near this place, but I didn't see who was shooting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Could you just -- I know you showed us yesterday approximately where the prisoner was when he got shot. Can you just please use the same model and show us approximately where you were when the prisoner got shot?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Right there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Just let the record reflect the witness is pointing --

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: It happened there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The witness is pointing -- I'm sorry, I don't see the number. The number of the little white house? Building B.

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: In the grassy area across from building B.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And what were you doing at the time that the prisoner was shot? Please sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I happened to be outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So you were just standing there watching; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And approximately how long had you been there, one minute, 15 minutes, before the prisoner was actually shot?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, you said that this happened when a large group of prisoners had been brought in after some combat operations. Could it have been when the prisoners were brought in after the operation in Bradina?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: They were brought, I think, from Gorodznic (Phon), Biljelnik (Phon). I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You stated there was a large number of them. Were some of them lined up against the wall --

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, is it your testimony that when you were there none of the prisoners were being beaten immediately before the prisoner tried to escape; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Did you hear any noises, sounds that would have been consistent with the prisoners being beaten?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, besides you, who else who worked in the camp was present at the time this prisoner was shot?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Velija Mujo, and I think another Velija Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you remember if Mr. Delic was there?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, did you have a weapon at that time?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you ever have a weapon when you worked in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but only when I used my car outside when I went to fulfil some duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Would the guards have weapons?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but not all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you stated that the person was warned, I believe, two times to stop. Did you hear that yourself?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Who issued the warning?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Probably the soldiers who were close to him, but it was not the people from our facilities. It was some people from Bosnia, from Foca, I don't know exactly, maybe Miljevina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that the prisoner was being asked questions. Could you hear the questions being asked?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Rarely.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, I'm referring to the time that the prisoner was shot. You stated that he was being asked -- yesterday you stated that he was being asked questions before he escaped. Did you hear the questions?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what happened after the shooting? What happened to the body? Was there a report? Please tell us what happened after the person was killed?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't look at it, and I didn't come close to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And so it was a matter of no interest to you whatsoever what happened to the body or anything about the killing?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I really do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you stand around for a few minutes to watch what happened or you weren't interested or just --

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I went into the building immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. And why did you go into the building?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: What do I know? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, have you ever heard of Miroslav Vujicic. Could he have been the person who was shot?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I knew the people of different ethnic backgrounds, not very well in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, you also talked about the murder of Mr. Susic. Was there any investigation into the murder of Mr. Susic?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, were you ever given any instructions about how to behave in the camp or even what you were supposed to do if a prisoner tried to escape?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: We always received orders from the superior command that we shouldn't beat or murder or do any harm to any prisoner, any prisoner, wherever we would go, that was the first thing that we were told.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And who from the superior command told you that?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I could have been told this by Rale Musinovic and I don't know who he was told that by.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you receive this instruction orally or in writing?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: For the most part orally.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you ever see anything in writing about the treatment of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Maybe, maybe.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were you ever told anything about your weapon, was your weapon to be kept with the safety on or off?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How is that relevant?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I believe there has been some testimony about that or that there's going to be with respect to one of the witnesses who may be upcoming, so that's why I am specifically asking that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How long does it take?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Microphone not on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If the witness doesn't know, I certainly won't pursue it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were you ever given any instructions about how your weapon was to be kept with the safety on or off?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I always had it on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And were you ever given any instructions one way or the other?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: There was no need.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, during the time you were at the camp, are you aware of any guard ever being disciplined for anything?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Maybe, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, in addition to Mrs. Cecez and Mrs. Antic, there were other women in the camp, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Zilic (Phon) and another one or two, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you talked about where the women were kept and you said the women could use the bathroom freely. Did the women have to ask the guards' permission to use the bathroom or could they use it even without asking the guards' permission?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: They had to ask permission from the guards. Also because it was locked so that nobody could come to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, when the weather was nice, the guards sometimes were not in the actual reception area, but spent time outside of that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: The most part there was someone there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: But sometimes, depending on the weather, the guards would be outside, correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: For the most part, they were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can I ask that the witness be shown again, Defence Exhibit 27-3. That's the chart that we saw yesterday. Can we have it on the ELMO, please. Now, sir, you indicated yesterday that the one door -- one door was permanently barricaded, the door that led directly from where the women were kept to the main hall; was that correct? And can you just point this out again for the judges, show them the door that was barricaded all the time.

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, even today.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can you just use the one to your right, sir, just because it -- can you just show it on that one. Okay, show the door that was always barricaded. Okay. And so when the women wanted to go to the bathroom or were brought outside to clean, they would go through the guard room and then out through the hallway into the bathroom, correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Correct. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, let me, the window in the guard room that's closest to the main hall, can you point that out for one second. I'm sorry, the one that's closest to the main hall, the other window. I'm sorry, are there three windows there that you see, sir?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you please point to the window that's closest to the main hall. Yes, that window, sir. Now, sir, you would agree with me that you could see Tunnel No. 9 from that window, couldn't you? If you know.

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: A guard, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a minute before you go any further. The women were kept in the room which is marked as "Weapons."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We're more concerned with the window in that room.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I believe and I have just reviewed the testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: They would not be staying long in the guard room on the way to the bathroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that the testimony will reflect this, but I believe that the women stated that they did sometimes look out of the guard room, especially because the guards were sometimes outside and they were permitted to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: All of the guards or some of the guards?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That there was nobody in the guard room on occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Well, ask him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I have asked him that. He said sometimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He said sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Maybe there are two guards, one is left behind and the other went out. You haven't clarified that position. Maybe they are taking turns.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, do you know whether or not there was always one guard in the guard room or is it sometimes the case that sometimes the guards would be outside?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: All the guards.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: All the guards?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Always one.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And how do you know that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Frankly, these are matters of speculation. None of the guards is before us, so I don't see why you are pressing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That's fine, I'll go forward.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever learn that some of the women had been sexually assaulted while they were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You never heard any reports or stories that there had been any sexual mistreatment at all; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, at the time you went with Mr. Delic as his assistant to look for the Antic weapons, was Mr. Delic on crutches at that time?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Certainly he was able to walk in -- at least he was able to walk?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, you talked about the report that you and Mr. Delic signed regarding the weapons. Who typed this report?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I believe it was Delic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, I know that it was your first report and you may not have been familiar with sort of techniques about how exactly to prepare a report, but let me ask you, did you think that it was important to be truthful in the report?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was truthful except that we didn't put in a name of the sister of the person who was accused of having had the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So, is it truthful that, and if you want to see this document again, we can get it for you. Was it truthful when you stated, "When we arrived at the spot, Cedo showed us the places where he had been hiding the rifles"?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Correct, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So it was Mr. Antic who showed you where the rifles were, not Mrs. Antic? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: His sister told us that also.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So that they both showed you where the same rifle was? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: How do you mean the same?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, in your report, you indicate that Mr. Antic showed you the places where he had been hiding the rifles and you now say that Mr. Antic did show you both places and Mrs. Antic also showed you one place. And so my question is, it's your testimony that both Mrs. Antic and her brother, Cedo Antic, showed you the spot, the same spot where the same rifle was buried; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: The places were shown, first Cedo showed the place where his rifle was and then she showed where her rifle was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, if that's the case, sir, then would you agree with me that the statement, "When we arrived at the spot, Cedo showed us the places where he had been hiding the rifles." That that's incorrect?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is also correct, both things are correct. What we did is just omit his sister because we believed that it was not necessary to include it in the report. But now I am saying that she was there too because that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And you're saying that you had two different people show you the same spot where the same rifle was buried; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object, that's a mischaracterisation of the evidence. He's been pretty clear on that, there's two different rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did Mr. Antic show you where only one rifle was or did he show you where both rifles were?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: We were told where both rifles were, but the sister went to the cherry tree next to the fence to show where that rifle was, the M-48 rifle.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, let me just try to be very clear. I have just a very simple question. When your report states, "Cedo showed us the places where he had been hiding the rifles." Is that correct or not correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And there were two rifles and Mr. Cedo showed you were both of them were; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you stated that you did not believe it was important to mention Mrs. Antic. Why did you at least think it was not important to mention Mrs. Antic?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: We were making that report for the first time, so that's how I thought it should be done. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, did you think maybe the rifle wasn't hers and that's why it wasn't important to mention her? Just why did you think it was important to mention Mr. Antic and not Mrs. Antic?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: We didn't know until she confessed. There were other -- she had two rifles, we found one and Atia (Phon) found another one. We found this one because she told us where it was. And Atia (Phon) found the other one.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was her report written before or after her "confession"?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: After she confessed, when we brought in the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, I assume that you have no idea why another driver who worked at the camp would have stated to this Chamber that the only persons who raped women in the camp were Mr. Delic and yourself. I assume you don't have any idea why someone might have stated that?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me speak for a moment about Mrs. Cecez's interrogation. Now, you stated that you were told by Mr. Rale Musinovic to interrogate Mrs. Cecez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And you were supposed to interrogate her about where her husband was; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were you supposed to interrogate her about anything else?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: In Donje Selo and the people there who had the weapons, where did they hide them, who left, where did they go to and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did this interrogation take place soon after Mrs. Cecez had been brought to the camp?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: (No translation).

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Is it correct that Mrs. Cecez was first kept in the administration building for several days and then moved to the reception building?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: That is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Please tell us where she was kept the entire time then. Is your testimony that she was always kept in the reception building? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think he pointed to a room within that building and it should be identified on the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was there. It was there, because before that, two other women were there. There was Najana (Phon) and another one.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, was the military investigation committee working in Celebici the -- well, in the beginning when you first got to the camp or did they come later?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Not right away. After the reception of the prisoners and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, was the commission -- were they working in Celebici at the time that Mrs. Cecez was brought to the camp?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, when you interrogated Mrs. Cecez, was it during the day or during the night?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand, was it during the day or the night?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: When was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Daytime.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. And where did the interrogation take place?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: In a command building.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. And would you be able to, if I showed you a diagram or a model, would you be able to remember what room?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You have a smaller model of the administration block of the command building, maybe it could be useful to have it before us. First ask him, does it look like the command room?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I will. I just want to go back to my seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise that as a model of the command building? The administration building, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, can you please tell us and I think that they are marked on the inside, can you point and tell us the number or the letter of the room where you interrogated Mrs. Cecez?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I am not sure, but it was either this or that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you just look for me, sir, and are there numbers or notations on the room numbers that you can tell us which of the two rooms?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Twelve or eleven. I can't recall exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, who else was present in their room at any time during the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Almir Mucic (sic), the policeman.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, did you write a report after this interrogation?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I had nothing to write because she didn't confess to anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the transcript again there's a notation of "Mr. Mucic" on line 14, page 43, that wasn't the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: There should be some care in these transcripts because there have been too many errors.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Is it Almir Muhic, sir, who was present during the interrogation? I'm sorry, could you just repeat the name again, there's just some issue in the transcript. Who was the other person --

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Almir Nuhic, Almir Nuhic, A-l-m-i-r N-u-h-i-c, a policeman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I want to ask a question. Who asked you to interrogate Mrs. Cecez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My commanding officer, Rale Musinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There was already an investigative military commission there who could interrogate her? Why was this task specifically given to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rale Musinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This is not the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am going to ask that again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, let me just ask a couple of preliminary questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You were aware that Mrs. Cecez was being kept in the camp as a hostage because they wanted her husband, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Because of the husband and because of herself because she was hiding it and she was behaving like everyone else.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just please explain what you mean when you say she was hiding it and she was behaving like everyone else?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Because the night when we came to Donje Selo, she and her husband did not come out, but she was with them and she shot, she was firing like everyone else. And she didn't -- and she wouldn't have needed to flee from us. Why did she flee and hide?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, is it your testimony that Mrs. Cecez was shooting during the attack on Donje Selo?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: It is possible. I did not see it. It is possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And you would agree with me that there were many, many women who fled when Donje Selo was being attacked.

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Not many. There were women down there, nobody did anything to those who stayed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You would agree with me that there were a number of women besides Mrs. Cecez who fled from Donje Selo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But he didn't arrest her, how would he know why she was arrested. The fact is that she was arrested, but how would he know? That question should be directed to the person who arrested her.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, now you stated that you gave Mrs. Cecez flowers, was this before or after Mrs. Antic came to the camp?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Before and after.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And did you bring Mrs. Antic flowers too or just Mrs. Cecez?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Only Mrs. Cecez.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, had you known Mrs. Cecez before you started working in the camp?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, she worked in a kiosk in front of the department store, the kiosk selling newspapers and similar things.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So you knew each other from before and both of you recognised each; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: A little bit, but we knew each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will now rise and come back at noon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly remind the witness he is still under his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Witness Djacic, may I remind you that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Ms. McHenry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I am just about finished, but I want to advise you and the witness that during the break Ms. Residovic informed me with respect to one issue about the food. There were some potentially important interpretation problems. So I am going to go over some of those same questions based on what Ms. Residovic and Mr. Kuzmanovic have informed me. So I will be repeating some of my questions, because, as I understand it, there may be an issue that even affects the meaning of what it said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, let me just -- I've been asked. Can you please move your chair forward a little bit so the interpreters can hear your voice better. Can you move your chair a little bit forward. Okay. Now, sir, can you just once again explain, when the food came for the prisoners, how was it actually given to the prisoners? And I know I am asking you to repeat some of what you said before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Perhaps you might --

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Every facility had their own mess tins. Zlatan Ustalic, when he would bring the food to Celebici, the young man, Sok, would carry out the mess tins and bring them to a gate where there were three to four women. And the same people -- the people would come from the facilities to take the food, and this food would be taken to the facilities. And ten persons from every facility, depending on how many there were, would come out and eat. The food would come twice a day. And warm food would come twice a day and cooked food would come twice a day, and dry food, uncooked food, would come once a day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, what I wanted to find out was are you asking him how the food is distributed when they arrive?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think this fairly sums it up.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, sir, when Mr. Ustalic would bring the food, what gate was it that the mess tins -- can you just show us on the chart where it was that the food would be brought and distributed to the three or four people who would come to take the food.

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: The guards would carry the food at the gate, since there were three to four women there. And they would use a tray, just like at a hotel, and they would carry whatever food there was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And did all this happen in the area around the administration building?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: The food was distributed close to the administration building.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And if I understand you, it would come in large containers, and then there would be trays with ten smaller containers that then would be brought to the hangar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Every hangar had their own mess tins, and people would come to get these mess tins and the bread, and they would take them to the facility. There were some stools in front of the facilities and the meal would be completed there, and then everything would be returned back to the main building.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, my question is: After it was -- the food was given -- the food comes and it's sort of initially distributed around the administration building, in that area. Is it the case, then, that these very large mess tins would be brought to hangar number 6, or is it the case that these ten smaller containers would be brought to hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Depending on how many people there were in the hangar. There were -- more people were going if there were more people in the hangar. More people would go to get the food. Sometimes I helped to carry the bread.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And then when the food ran out, would the prisoners have to go back to the administration building to refill the containers with more food?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: If there was any food, they could do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, normally would -- would it normally, on an average occasion, would the prisoners have to go back to the administration building to get the containers filled up again, or would it be sufficient just to do it one time?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: If there was a need, they would go back.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me go forward, sir. Now --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, since this question was already asked and the witness more than once used the word "mess tin," which is used to carry the food, maybe I should suggest to my colleague to ask the witness what this mess tin is, which was used to carry the food to the facility. Since this again -- there is some unclarity around this term, and this is a concrete term for some kind of a container.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the problem is -- she is using the word manerca (Phon), which, as I understand it, is a great big pot that you would have a lot of food in, where a mess tin is something that an individual soldier would eat out of. It would be a much smaller thing. So what you have would be the difference between a pot with food for a whole bunch of people, that it would be dished out to individual people in smaller containers. I think that's where the confusion is coming from.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me ask the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, can you just, even with your hands, approximate the size of the containers that the food would come in when Mr. Ustalic brought it? What kind of size are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Fifty litres.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And then when it was brought to the prisoners, was it brought in those 50 litre containers, or was it moved to those 10 smaller containers that were then brought to the hangar?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Zlatan brought them in the larger containers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And when the food was actually brought from the administration area to the hangar, was it brought in those large 50 litre containers, or was it put in 10 smaller containers, and then the 10 smaller containers were brought to the hangar?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: No, not in the smaller ones. Just in the larger ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So the prisoners would go up to the administration building and get one or more 50 litre containers and then bring it back to the hangar?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And when you refer to the 10 containers that were available to the hangar, what are those containers?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Those are plates or dishes or a little bit larger. And we also used them to eat from them. It stayed behind after the JNA on the compound.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. I am moving forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let me clarify a bit. From the witness's testimony, it appears only representatives of each particular group of detainees go up to receive the food. Am I right? Not everybody goes up?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Depending on who was on duty, and they would take turns. Today, one group of prisoners; tomorrow, another group of prisoners would do the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Now, the important thing is whether, when they take this food, they serve everybody in their group. It means they serve everyone in the group of each of the representatives?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: So if it is not sufficient for them the first time, perhaps they come back a second time to serve the other ones who did not have enough at the beginning?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Mostly they carried as much as was needed the first time, because we knew, considering with respect to the number of people there were in each facility, how much was necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, is the reason that you gave Mrs. Cecez flowers because you felt bad about how you treated her?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: God forbid.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, why did you give Mrs. Cecez flowers, then?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Because I spent more time there talking, because she asked me to be there, and she talked about all kinds of things about her daughter, how she was in Vojvodina somewhere, things like that. So whatever was nice, she talked to me about. She saw the flowers through the window and she asked me if she could get two or three roses, and I did that a couple of times, and I brought those roses to her.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was there a bed in the room where you interrogated Mrs. Cecez?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You would agree with me that in the rooms used by the military investigation commission there were not beds, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: Where the commission worked, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Cecez, was supposed to be raped as part of her interrogation, wasn't she?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You've already testified that you were a simple driver with no experience interrogating persons, and that the investigating commission was made up of professionals. Just explain to us, please, what is it that you could do to Mrs. Cecez to make her give information that the investigative commission would not have been able to do better? Why were you chosen?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I was the closest to my commanding officer, Rale Musinovic, and he told me, "Please, go outside and investigate Grozdana Cecez, where she was, what she did, why she did not surrender this weapon, where her husband was," and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Why didn't the military investigation commission do this, sir, which was made up of professionals?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object to that. That's speculation on the part of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If you know, sir.

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: I don't understand anything now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: My question is, if you know, why was a driver, with no experience interrogating people, chosen to investigate Mrs. Cecez, rather than the military investigation commission that was made up of professionals?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think this is a question for the persons who sent --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I said if he knows. If he doesn't know, he can state that.

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: At that point in time there was no commission, when she arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, right before the break you stated on several occasions that the military investigation commission was operating at the time Mrs. Cecez was brought in. Are you now changing that testimony?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: The commission wasn't there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So you are saying that they were operating, but they just didn't happen to be in the camp in the daytime when you interrogated her; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: What is correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR DJAJIC
utterances.text: That I interrogated her.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: My question is: You've already stated that the military investigation committee was operating at the time Mrs. Cecez was brought in. You remember saying that?
