utterances.text: You know, since you shifted from the Durham (Phon) rule, the story has always been there. Everybody knows what a particular Defence, which is based on insanity, are not listed. This is your problem, because the Durham (Phon) rule is generally used in the Americans --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: This is not insanity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: This is a passion insanity.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it's a different defence completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Okay, diminished responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Okay. Go and read it again in the American jurisdiction. Go ahead and read it again.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: It's not an American jurisdiction. It's in British jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I don't have to argue with you. But I am telling you, the shift has always been from both sides of the Atlantic, not only from Scotland, from Britain, from US, from Canada, they have always been the same. And it is not new, even in the United States. It's there. So if you really say you have been using it with the case law jurisdiction there, then pick it up. And from what you have said, you have now pleaded it, you need the facts on which you are pleading. If those are the facts on which you rely, plead it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: No Court can give you a finding on a question of law in a vacuum.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: In a vacuum, no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Produce the evidence and we will see.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am going to assume that we will go with the most widely accepted, basic definition, and I will proceed based upon that assumption on my part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That's for you to decide what evidence to lead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Don't be too introspective about it or feel that it is a closed jurisdiction. The law has been very clearly stated since 1957. It's clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You are right, the Homicide Act in Great Britain of 1957 was very clear, and I'm glad you gave me an indication of that. Thank you. I think I have a clearer view on what it is I am looking for, anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I thought you knew it when you were pleading it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't study the 1957 Homicide Act in our law school in our country because we do not have a defence of diminished mental capacity in the United States. We have a mitigation of punishment, but we do not have a defence. So thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to do something much simpler now. We have a request, which we have submitted to the Trial Chamber. The Prosecutor has heard the Defence of Mr. Delalic, and he now already probably knows whether there will be a replica to that defence. Our request is, if this is certain and if they know which evidence they are going to lead, that they should, according to their duties based on Article 66, to let us know about that. And with regard to your respect, I would like you -- I would like to ask you to tell us under which -- in which deadlines this should be done based on your ruling. I would like to say that so far we have received no response by the Prosecution to take our request into the -- into consideration, and I would like for us -- for all of us to be ready to do our task within this deadline. And therefore I would like to ask you to take this request into consideration and to issue an order, if the Prosecution decides to replicate the defence of Mr. Delalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I thought you argued the motion about the limitation of your defence and losing your case and all that accompanied it. I think -- there is a decision on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think she is referring to rebuttal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not talking about that request. I -- we submitted a request which should demand from the Prosecution to state whether they will have rebuttal with regard to Mr. Delalic, that all our evidence -- that all the evidence is shown to us and that we are given the witness names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: (No microphone) -- that motion, whether there would be rebuttal or -- they were all in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It may be premature for the Prosecution to respond to your request. The witness is still being examined. Some of the witnesses, just like today also, spoke about Mr. Delalic. Maybe when the Prosecution -- the Defence evidence is over, the Prosecution will have a clearer picture whether to lead evidence in rebuttal or not. Also, some of the witnesses spoke about that role of Delalic to produce certificates. The lady here -- that he was not holding any particular office. Maybe some of the witnesses produced by the other defendants made something about the role of Mr. Delalic in the affair. So until the whole evidence is over, how can we ask the Prosecutor to give an undertaking or make a statement that he will produce or not produce any evidence in rebuttal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It's a joint trial, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But this is the difficulty with the Prosecutor. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are not -- we do not want to interfere with the Prosecution's work. The Prosecution will do what they will do at the end of evidence. We would just like to know after that, the deadlines within which this distinguished Tribunal will give us to prepare for our rejoinder. And, therefore, in our request there were some deadlines stated for your order which would give us this opportunity to -- which would help this Court be fairer to everybody the way it was so far. And we are all here now in this courtroom and, therefore, I want to just to make sure that we have time if the Prosecutor uses his right to prepare for the rejoinder and for the closing statements. That was the essence of our statement, so that we can prepare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We can only give an estimate of the prosecutor after we know how many days Ms. McMurrey is going to take in leading in evidence. Then we'll have a better idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Well, since the Prosecution will, if he does exercise his rights about rebuttals, then when he informs the Trial Chamber, they will know how to fix the time scale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: (Microphone not on).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: When he exercises his rights, then we'll know what he has to do, because it will never be through the prejudice of any other...

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. That is precisely what I was hoping to hear. As you are well aware, we cannot prepare our rejoinder overnight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I received a letter from the Prosecution which I responded to today. I think Ms. Boler is getting the reports from the two Dutch doctors right now. Only last weekend, the Italian forensic, I mean, clinical psychologist completed his testing of Mr. Landzo. That report has now been sent to all of the psychiatrists and they will be writing a report which should be available within the week. I just don't have it yet and they couldn't write their report until they had the findings of the clinical psychologist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: And how many other witnesses do you intend to examine? Just an idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I think I have -- well, that is one of the next issues I have. I am having a very difficult time getting my witnesses to come to The Hague. I have the outstanding subpoena duces tecum here., But I filed a new subpoena for witnesses that I have not subpoenaed before. We're having a difficult time. I filed another motion for leave of court to file to call additional witnesses to replace some of the witnesses that I may or may not be able to call. So I attached to this leave of Court to call additional witnesses. The same kind of notice that the Prosecution gave us. These are witnesses we will call, these are witnesses we may call, but I won't call any more than 20 fact witnesses, okay. I don't know which ones they're going to be until we see whether we get the subpoenas issued and who is going to be able to come. But I won't call any more than 20 fact witnesses. And that means there are three or four expert witnesses. So I really expect to be concluded by the first week in August, August 1, really. Based upon the way all the other testimonies have gone also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, it depends on how much you understand your case. That is the most important thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I also wanted to ask the Court another question. Mr. Hawking and victim and witnesses have brought to my attention that we are set to start July 13th. There is no way they can bring any of my witnesses to The Hague until the night of July 13th, because there's no housing from even as far as Rotterdam due to the jazz festival.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Maybe they can be accommodated in Rotterdam because it's only about 20 minutes drive.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I believe the victim and witnesses has taken that into account already and they've said that there is really no way. At that point, of course, I would have to rent a car or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You may not have the comforts of The Hague, but it's within drivable distance.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: If we start July 13th, I am predicting that we'll be through within two and a half weeks based upon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Before you enter the length of a trial you should know exactly what they are about to say, that determines how long it will take.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it also determines on the amount of the cross-examination from the prosecution. I can give my best guess, but I can't narrow it down to the minute and the second. And I don't think that I should be asked to at this point. I am doing the best I can to organise this ahead of time so we don't have any glitches when we come there. Also going back to the subpoena duces tecum, which the order on Friday asked me to answer two questions for the Court. And one of the questions is answered here. Friday afternoon I faxed to the Bosnian Embassy the question about the Konjic hospital. Ms. Vividovic (Phon) from the Bosnian Embassy, contacted the Deputy Minister of Health in Sarajevo. And I have a signed document here from the Deputy Minister of Health in Sarajevo stating the status -- it's not a hospital in Konjic, it's a health centre. And it says that it did not exist before the war, but it was formed during the war as a war hospital and it is within the net of war hospitals. Work on war hospitals was legal and those hospitals consisted of a net of war hospitals that ceased to exist after the Dayton agreement was signed in 1995. So now it's considered a health centre in Konjic, not a hospital, and it says we cannot confirm for sure whether a hospital will be registered there within the net of health institutions, but they don't believe so. So, at this point, to re-urge my request for the important medical documents that I believe are in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Where are those documents then?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: We don't have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You have to tell us where those documents are before you can ask us to produce them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, I think the question was, if it's not a state hospital, can you order the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We can ask the Bosnian government for assistance in getting the subpoena served on persons or institutions within the state.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, the Bosnian Embassy and the Ministry of Health cannot confirm that that is a state hospital at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You have to give the correct address. You have to give the correct description.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Even if it's a health centre, it's still within the jurisdiction of the State.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now I think we have satisfied every type of a requirement needed. We cannot get the documents, that we have to directly subpoena duces tecum the health centre in Konjic and ask the custodian of record or Dr. Buturovic to bring them with him when he comes, since he was the doctor who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You ask the doctor where the record is, maybe he can give you an indication. You see, this institution, whatever you call it, is within the territorial limits of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina and you can always request them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: But the question of the Court to me was, was it a state hospital? My answer is that the Bosnian embassy says it's not a state hospital. And also as far as Dr. Buturovic goes, may I let Ms. Boler respond to that, because we have tried as the team, the team of Delic has tried. He will not talk to us. He will not respond to us. And the medical records of Mr. Landzo, Mirko Babic and Branko Gotovac have not been secured at this point and I find them very necessary for the Defence of this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: And you want such a witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. He did the surgery on Mr. Landzo's hand. As a fact witness, I would never ask him to form an opinion coming adversely. As a fact witness, I need him to testify about the injuries to Mr. Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Maybe you've not paid his wife's fee.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have turned that over to the registry. That's in the registry's hands, not mine. Well, arrangements will be made to ensure that you get your witness, but you have to be sure that it is not a hostile witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'll take him as a hostile witness. I'll take him any way we can bring him. But besides the issue of the subpoena duces tecum, which I assume that the Court will issue some kind of order if I give you the address of the health centre in Konjic, that we need those documents because they're very important and this is 10 days before I am to start my trial basically. And I would like to have those documents or at least to know that we're in the process of securing those documents. I suppose the Court will render some kind of written order on that some time soon because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you have applied for a subpoena, you get in touch with John Hawkings. We'll sign the subpoena.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. I applied on June 22nd, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Only on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That was the 26th.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: No, no, no. June 22nd was the Monday we got back from our week off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think the first I heard of it was about 6.30 p.m. on Friday, the 26th.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, That's my new subpoena for the testifying witnesses. The subpoena duces tecum was filed June 22nd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You didn't even give particulars of the hospital and they're not appropriate designation of the documents you want.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I specifically said on the Monday we returned back that we need the medical records of three people. That's as specific as I can get. I don't have, you know, registration numbers or cause numbers because the doctor refuses to talk to us. And when my investigator goes to the office of records there, they say that the documents have been checked out. And there's no record of him. I mean, there's record that they existed, but somebody else has them in their possession. I can bring my investigator here to testify about that if you'd like to hear from him, but Ms. Boler just returned last night from Bosnia and I would like to ask the Court to hear what she has to say about this because these are really important for the Defence, if you will listen to Ms. Boler.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will just state that I spent the last few days in Bosnia and got back last night. Certainly discussed this with our investigator, Mr. Asim Suto and also discussed the same thing five or six weeks ago when I was there and in between. So we've been trying for quite some time to get these records. And Mr. Suto told me that, even five or six weeks ago when I was there previously, that he tried to get these records on several occasions and that Dr. Buturovic would not give them these records for the reasons that you just mentioned, Judge John and maybe some other ones also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I wasn't serious.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: But I think that that was pretty much exactly what Dr. Buturovic told our investigator. Also, talked to Mr. Suto again yesterday since I was there to see if he had had any subsequent luck getting those records from Dr. Buturovic. And, clearly, we are unable to get these records. The reason I talked about it again yesterday with Mr. Suto is because Cynthia faxed me a copy of your order. I was aware yesterday, you know, that there was some urgency for us to respond to this order. So I just, unless you have any questions, I think that's all I have got to add to, just to verify that we are indeed trying to get those records and cannot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is there any evidence that the doctor has the records himself?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I don't know new evidence, but I can tell you that Mr. Suto told me that Dr. Buturovic told him -- I may not be able to quote exactly what he said -- but, basically, I am not going to give you those records. I believe that Dr. Buturovic does have access to those records and I believe that he's withholding those records from us and I think that's...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let's see what a subpoena on him would do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, I have one quote from my investigator too. When he asked Dr. Buturovic about getting the records, Dr. Buturovic said, "You'll have to see my wife about that." And I can represent that's what my investigator told me. And this was on my November trip -- no, that was my February trip to Bosnia when I was trying to get the records at that point. But I would like to ask the Court if the Court would like for me to re-file another subpoena duces tecum with the address of the hospital or whether I can just file a supplement to this subpoena with the address and maybe more specificity, whatever you would like, I need to get this taken care of as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Get in touch with John Hawkings, the more up to date the address and all the particulars and so that we will follow it up.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I would be happy to do that. Thank you very much. Now, the motion that I did file at the 11th hour on Friday was the motion to subpoena -- no, motion for leave -- no, I just filed these today, Your Honour. I'm sorry, these have been filed today. It's a subpoena duces tecum -- I mean, a regular subpoena for the witnesses to come testify and the leave of court to add the additional witnesses and that was based on my conversation with Ms. Boler at two o'clock this morning when she slid these things under my door telling me that these witnesses refused to come without a subpoena. So I stayed out of court this morning to draw these up so that we are not wasting the Court's time, but I feel that it's very necessary. I don't want to wait any longer to discuss the issue of these subpoenas because I would like to start my case on time and I would like to have my witnesses that I need present in The Hague. So based on what Ms. Boler represented to me from her conversations with these witnesses over the last three days, it's necessary for us to issue the subpoenas if we want them to appear in The Hague. And this was just filed this morning after our return from writing them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will see to it. And we will look at it and see if -- well, I think we will try and help.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I appreciate help right now, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think that's all we have on the record. Because there is -- we've cleared all the motions. Some of them are not really necessary motions, given your hearing, merely because you were a little agitated, though some of them need not be filed at all. So we will rise and reassemble at 3.00 p.m. tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I just wanted to assure the Court that I don't file any motion that I don't feel is necessary for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The one on the diminished responsibility was not necessary. If we have anything for tomorrow morning, I don't think we do, we'll reassemble at 3.00 p.m. tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, I thank you very much for accommodating my visit --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: p.m. To be reconvened on Wednesday, the 1st of July, 1998 at 3.00 p.m.
